land.text: the Socialist Republic of Croatia, one of the federation's republics, whose independence the page dates to 25 June 1991

predecessors.note: Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991 and implemented it after the three-month moratorium ended on 8 October 1991 (Croatia page). The Serb-held third of the country passed to the Republic of Serbian Krajina (rebel dossier republic-of-serbian-krajina) until 1995-1998.

correction.text: Croatia in the year of its declaration of independence (25 June 1991), the land under government control: the same outline as the corrected 1992 shape, only the years change; the Serb-held third lay outside it

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria starts Croatia only in 1992 although the Croatia page dates the declaration to 25 June 1991. The War page says that 'one month after Croatia declared its independence' Serb forces 'held something less than one-third of the Croatian territory'.

correction.text: the Republic of Croatia of 1992-1995 without the Serb-held Krajina: Cliopatria's 1992 shape minus the Bosnian land it spills over (about 5,800 km2 of Bosnia and Herzegovina measured against Natural Earth) and minus the Knin area, which the shape still includes

keyframe_review.note: 1992-1995, 44,390 km2. The infobox gives 56,561 km2 (text 56,594); the War page gives the RSK as 13,913 km2 in early 1992, which leaves about 42,650 km2, ratio 1.04 to the shape, so the size agrees. But the outline is coarse (103 vertices): it takes in most of Sibensko-Kninska county (Knin, the RSK's capital) and 23 gazetteer cells of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I read as Croat-held Herzeg-Bosnia (dossier croatian-republic-of-herzeg-bosnia, 1991-1994), not Croatia. The Konavle strip near Dubrovnik (680 km2) was also occupied until October 1992 (ledger).

minus.text: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia, under UN transitional administration

correction.text: Croatia of 1996-1997 without Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia, which the Erdut Agreement put under the UN until its return in January 1998; applies to 1996-1997 only, from 1998 the new keyframe republic-of-croatia_1998 (the unchanged Cliopatria 1996 shape) holds

keyframe_review.note: 1996-2023, 52,453 km2, ratio 0.93 to the infobox 56,561 km2 (the rest is the islands and coast the outline leaves out). The shape already contains 8 of the 9 gazetteer cells of Vukovarsko-Srijemska county, but the page says the UNTAES 'transitional period began on 15 January 1996' and the territory 'was formally returned to Croatia' in 1998 (Croatia page: 'concluding with the UNTAES mission in January 1998'), so for 1996-1997 that land is not yet Croatian.

correction.text: the whole Republic of Croatia after the return of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia: Cliopatria's 1996 shape unchanged, only the years differ from the 1996-1997 correction

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the shape holds from January 1998 ('concluding with the UNTAES mission in January 1998'). The Neum strip of Bosnia and Herzegovina cuts the Dubrovnik coast off by land ('separated on land by a short coastline strip belonging to Bosnia and Herzegovina around Neum'); the shape's four Bosnian gazetteer cells are outline noise and are not corrected.
2024, identical to the 1996 shape; no change of border is on the page between 1998 and 2024 (Croatia joined NATO in April 2009, the EU in July 2013, the euro area and Schengen in 2023).

ledger.note: 1991, 25 June: Croatia declares independence from Yugoslavia. 'Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991.' Full implementation waited until a three-month moratorium ended on 8 October 1991; the EEC recognised Croatia on 15 January 1992. The page gives no boundary; the region is the government-held land of the corrected 1992 shape.

region.text: the Serb-held Krajina: Knin, Kordun, Banovina and western Slavonia, 'less than one-third of the Croatian territory' a month after the declaration

ledger.note: 1991: war over the Serb-held third of Croatia. 'One month after Croatia declared its independence', Serb forces 'held something less than one-third of the Croatian territory'. Infobox: war 'March 1, 1991 - November 12, 1995'. The page names no first campaign; July is the page's 'one month after' 25 June.

region.text: the Serb-held Krajina, later the Republic of Serbian Krajina

ledger.note: 1991: Croatia loses control of the Krajina. Serb forces hold 'something less than one-third of the Croatian territory' a month after the declaration; the RSK itself was proclaimed in December 1991 (Krajina page).

region.text: another 680 square kilometres of occupied territory near Dubrovnik (Konavle), held by the Yugoslav army and not part of the RSK

ledger.note: 1991, October: Konavle near Dubrovnik is occupied by the Yugoslav army. The War page gives the territory ('another 680 square kilometers (260 sq mi) of occupied territory near Dubrovnik') and its withdrawal in 1992; it dates the campaign that took it ('the Siege of Dubrovnik that started in October', 1991) but not Konavle's capture itself, so the land is my reading of the siege (reviewer eu-22-f: month and confidence 2 from that sentence; was confidence 1, year only).

region.text: SAO Western Slavonia, around Pakrac and Okucani

ledger.note: 1991, 19 December: Western Slavonia joins the Krajina. 'SAO Western Slavonia joined the RSK on 19 December 1991'; the page gives the joining, not the capture, so the loss of control may be earlier.

region.text: the Krajina front frozen by the ceasefire

ledger.note: 1992, January: the front is frozen. A UN-sponsored ceasefire 'was agreed on January 2, 1992, and came into force the next day' (the Sarajevo Agreement), and it 'became a lasting ceasefire'. UNPROFOR was created on 21 February 1992 (Resolution 743).

region.text: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia

ledger.note: 1992, 26 February: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia join the Krajina. The Krajina page lists them as 'added on 26 February 1992'; the page does not date the capture, so the loss may be earlier.

region.text: Konavle near Dubrovnik, restored to Croatian authorities

ledger.note: 1992, October: the Yugoslav army leaves Konavle. It withdrew 'between September 30 and October 20, 1992' and 'the remainder of Konavle was restored to the Croatian authorities'; the Prevlaka peninsula 'was demilitarized and turned over to the UNPROFOR'. By then the army was that of the rump Yugoslavia (dossier serbia-montenegro).

1995, May: Operation Flash. 'Croatian forces gained control of SAO Western Slavonia in Operation Flash (May).' The Krajina page gives the month only (the dossier republic-of-serbian-krajina gives 1-4 May from another page).
1995, May: Western Slavonia returns to Croatia in Operation Flash. 'Croatian forces gained control of SAO Western Slavonia in Operation Flash (May).'
1995, May: Flash ends with Western Slavonia in Croatian hands; the page gives the month of the operation, not its last day.

region.text: the Krajina, the biggest part of occupied Croatia

ledger.note: 1995, August: Operation Storm. Croatia retook 'the biggest part of occupied Croatia in Operation Storm (August)'.

region.text: the biggest part of occupied Croatia: Knin, Kordun, Banovina and northern Dalmatia

ledger.note: 1995, August: the Krajina falls to Croatia in Operation Storm. 'The RSK was disbanded and most of its Serb population (from 150,000 to 200,000 people) fled.' The War page: the offensives 'effectively ended the war in its favor'; the Croatia page: 'The war effectively ended in August 1995 with a decisive victory by Croatia.' The region is my reading of 'occupied Croatia'.
1995, August: Storm ends the fighting for the Krajina; the RSK's president's term ended on 7 August 1995 (page). The Erdut Agreement of 12 November 1995 settled the Eastern Slavonia remnant.

region.text: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia, the last occupied land

ledger.note: 1998, January: the last occupied land returns to Croatia. 'The remaining occupied areas were restored to Croatia following the Erdut Agreement ... concluding with the UNTAES mission in January 1998.' The Krajina page: the UN transitional period began on 15 January 1996 and the land 'was formally returned to Croatia' in 1998. Counterpart nobody: the RSK ended with the Erdut Agreement of 12 November 1995 (dossier republic-of-serbian-krajina, dissolve to nobody), and the land was under the UN transitional administration (UNTAES) from 15 January 1996 until 'in 1998, the UNTAES mission was complete and the territory was formally returned to Croatia' (Krajina page). Reviewer eu-22-f changed the counterpart from republic-of-serbian-krajina.

wars.name: Croatian War of Independence

zones.text: Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia

wars.outcome: Croatian victory: Croatian forces regained most of the RSK's territory in 1995; Eastern Slavonia, under UN control from 1996, was reintegrated by January 1998.
wars.note: Infobox 'March 1, 1991 - November 12, 1995'. The page: the RSK 'encompassed 13,913 square kilometers' in early 1992 (the Krajina page says 17,028 km2 at its greatest extent). The Slovenian conflict ended with the Brioni Agreement (freezing Croatia's declaration for three months).

wars.name: Operation Flash
wars.outcome: Croatian forces gained control of SAO Western Slavonia in May 1995.
wars.note: The page gives the month only.

wars.name: Operation Storm

zones.text: the biggest part of occupied Croatia

wars.outcome: Croatia retook the biggest part of the occupied land in August 1995; the RSK was disbanded and 150,000 to 200,000 Serbs fled.
wars.note: The page gives the month only; the day-level dates in the republic-of-serbian-krajina dossier come from another page.

certainty.note: Front lines of the war (to 1995) and the UN-administered Eastern Slavonia (1996-1997) are not treaty borders; the Prevlaka peninsula stayed disputed under UN observers (the War page: 'demilitarized and turned over to the UNPROFOR').

The borders are the former republican borders of Yugoslavia, but the Croatia page lists 'unresolved border disputes throughout Southeast Europe' including with Slovenia (Piran Bay); the sea border with Slovenia and the Neum corridor are the exceptions.

notes: Three pages opened (budget 1-2: the third was needed for the 1995 and 1998 border moves). Cliopatria's two shapes are not nested: the 1992 shape (44,390 km2) contains about 5,800 km2 of Bosnia and Herzegovina (read as Herzeg-Bosnia) and most of Sibensko-Kninska county including Knin, so the corrections subtract them; the 1996 shape contains Eastern Slavonia two years before the return (corrected for 1996-1997). Day-level dates for Flash and Storm are not on the pages opened (the Krajina dossier of another batch has 1-4 May and 4-7 August from a different page); only months are recorded here. Not settled for want of a page: the Prevlaka dispute with Serbia-Montenegro/Montenegro after 1992 (the pages say only 'demilitarized'), the Piran Bay border with Slovenia (page silent), the day the Konavle occupation began (reviewer eu-22-f dated it to October 1991 from the War page's 'Siege of Dubrovnik that started in October'), and presidents of Croatia (no list opened, so no rulers key). Region names the gazetteer lacks: Konavle (used as a 18 km radius at 42.55 N 18.30 E), Krajina (built from the difference of the two Cliopatria shapes plus a 35 km radius at Knin, 44.04 N 16.19 E), Pakrac/Okucani (30 km radius at 45.35 N 17.20 E). Legal and colour continuity: the Republic of Croatia is the successor of the Socialist Republic of Croatia inside the SFRY (dossier socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia); its predecessors in older dossiers (kingdom-of-croatia, independent-state-of-croatia) are different states.
